passages.A1_SAM: Sam lives in London. London is the capital city of England and of the United Kingdom. The River Thames goes through London. Every day Sam walks to school. He likes the red buses. On Saturdays he visits his grandmother in Cardiff, the capital city of Wales.
passages.A1_CAFE:
Waiter: Hello! What would you like?
Harry: A cup of tea, please.
Waiter: Anything to eat?
Harry: Yes, a cheese sandwich, please.
Waiter: That's four pounds.
Harry: Here you are. Thank you!
passages.A2_UK4: The United Kingdom is made up of four countries: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Their capital cities are London, Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast. 'Great Britain' is the name for England, Scotland and Wales together. Northern Ireland is on the island of Ireland.
passages.A2_GP:
Receptionist: Good morning, City Health Centre.
Sophie: Hello. I'd like to make an appointment with a doctor, please.
Receptionist: Are you registered with us?
Sophie: Yes, I am.
Receptionist: Is tomorrow at 10:30 OK?
Sophie: Yes, that's fine. Thank you.
passages.A2_TRAIN:
Passenger: A return ticket to Manchester, please.
Clerk: Travelling today?
Passenger: Yes, and I'll come back on Sunday.
Clerk: That's 45 pounds. The train leaves from platform 6 at 14:20.
Passenger: Thanks very much.
passages.B1_SAINTS: Each country of the UK has a patron saint with a special day. St David's Day, for Wales, is on 1 March. St Patrick's Day, for Northern Ireland, is on 17 March. St George's Day, for England, is on 23 April, and St Andrew's Day, for Scotland, is on 30 November. Only Scotland and Northern Ireland have their patron saint's day as an official holiday.
passages.B1_MAGNA: In 1215, King John was forced by his noblemen to agree to a number of their demands. The result was a charter of rights called the Magna Carta, which means 'Great Charter'. It established the idea that even the king was subject to the law. It protected the rights of the nobility and restricted the king's power to collect taxes or to make or change laws.
passages.B1_NHS: The National Health Service (NHS) began in 1948. Its aim was to give everyone in the UK healthcare that is free at the point of use. The minister responsible for setting it up was Aneurin (Nye) Bevan. To see a family doctor, called a GP, you usually need to register at a local surgery first.
passages.B1_POPPY: Remembrance Day, on 11 November, commemorates those who died fighting for the UK and its allies. It began after the First World War, which ended at 11 a.m. on 11 November 1918. People wear red poppies, and there is a two-minute silence at 11 a.m.
passages.B1_VOTE:
Officer: To vote, you need to be on the electoral register.
James: How old do I need to be?
Officer: For UK general elections you must be at least 18.
James: And how often are general elections held?
Officer: At least every five years.
passages.B2_ELIZ: Elizabeth I, the daughter of Henry VIII, became queen in 1558. She was popular with her people, partly because of the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588, a large fleet of ships sent by Spain to invade England. Her reign also saw a flowering of English drama, with playwrights such as William Shakespeare.
passages.B2_FIRE: In 1666 a fire broke out in a bakery in Pudding Lane and spread across much of the City of London, destroying thousands of houses and many churches, including St Paul's Cathedral. The architect Sir Christopher Wren was responsible for rebuilding St Paul's, which still stands today.
passages.B2_VOTES: During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, women campaigned for the right to vote. In 1903 Emmeline Pankhurst founded the Women's Social and Political Union, whose members became known as suffragettes. In 1918 women over the age of 30 were given the vote, and in 1928 women were given the vote at 21, the same age as men.
passages.C1_CHURCHILL: Winston Churchill became Prime Minister in 1940, at a time when much of Europe had fallen to Nazi Germany. He refused to surrender, and his speeches, including the promise that 'we shall fight on the beaches', helped to raise public morale. Although he was defeated in the general election of 1945, he returned as Prime Minister in 1951.
passages.C1_INDUSTRY: The Industrial Revolution, which began in Britain in the 18th century, transformed the way goods were produced. Machines powered by steam, using coal as fuel, replaced much work previously done by hand. Factories drew people from the countryside into rapidly growing cities, where working conditions were often harsh, and children as well as adults worked long hours.
passages.C1_PARKS:
Presenter: Should national parks charge entry fees?
Roza: I'm in favour. The money could fund conservation.
Paul: I see the logic, but fees risk excluding families on low incomes.
Roza: Then why not make entry free for local residents?
Paul: That might be a reasonable compromise.
passages.C2_DEVO: Since 1997 the UK has seen a significant devolution of power. The Scottish Parliament and the National Assembly for Wales (renamed the Senedd in 2020) were established in 1999, while the Northern Ireland Assembly emerged from the 1998 Good Friday Agreement. The devolved administrations legislate on areas such as health and education, whereas defence and foreign affairs remain reserved to the UK Parliament at Westminster.
passages.C2_SHAKES: Shakespeare's influence on the English language is hard to overstate. Hundreds of words and phrases are first recorded in his plays and poems. Yet a first recorded use is not proof of invention: some expressions may simply reflect the everyday speech of his time, which happens to survive in his writing. Scholars therefore caution against crediting him with every phrase popularly attributed to him.
passages.C2_PEAT: Peatlands cover only around 3% of the Earth's land surface, yet they are estimated to store more carbon than all the world's forests combined. When drained for agriculture, peat decomposes and releases this carbon, turning a vital sink into a significant source of emissions. Restoration by re-wetting drained bogs is therefore increasingly seen as a cost-effective climate measure.
passages.A1_ELLA: My name is Ella. I live in Edinburgh. Edinburgh is the capital city of Scotland. In the centre of the city there is a very old castle on a hill. On 31 December we celebrate Hogmanay, the Scottish New Year. We watch the fireworks with our family.
passages.A2_BONFIRE: Bonfire Night is on 5 November. It remembers an event in 1605. A group of Catholics, led by Guy Fawkes, planned to kill the Protestant king with a bomb in the Houses of Parliament. Their plan failed. Today people in Great Britain light bonfires and set off fireworks at home or at big public displays.
passages.B2_LAKES: The Lake District in north-west England is the country's largest national park. Its long, narrow lakes and steep valleys were carved by glaciers during the last Ice Age. Windermere is the biggest stretch of water, and Scafell Pike, at 978 metres, is the highest mountain in England. Sheep farming has shaped the landscape for centuries, and the area inspired the poet William Wordsworth.
passages.B2_INTERVIEW_UK:
Interviewer: Why do you want to work for us?
Amira: I've read about your work with refugees in Manchester, and I'd like to use my languages to help.
Interviewer: Which languages do you speak?
Amira: English, French and Arabic, and I'm learning Spanish.
Interviewer: Could you work at weekends?
Amira: Yes, as long as I know the rota a week in advance.
passages.C1_TOWER: Standing on the north bank of the River Thames, the Tower of London was begun by William the Conqueror soon after his victory at Hastings in 1066. Over the centuries it has served as a royal palace, a fortress and a prison, and it still houses the Crown Jewels. The Tower is guarded by the Yeoman Warders, popularly known as Beefeaters, and in 1988 it was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List.
passages.C2_LANGUAGES: English is not the only language with deep roots in the UK. Welsh, a Celtic language, is spoken by many people in Wales and is taught in its schools; in parts of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland, Gaelic is still spoken, while some people in Northern Ireland speak Irish Gaelic. English itself was shaped by successive arrivals: the Anglo-Saxons brought the Germanic dialects at its core, and after the Norman Conquest of 1066 French added words such as 'park' and 'beauty'.
